speaker: Brad Smith
title: An interview with Microsoft President Brad Smith
question: In enterprise technology governance, what structurally causes a company's stated ethical principles to collapse in practice?
guest: The most natural thing for any creative company to do is to just keep creating more products and keep selling them to anyone who will buy them. Yet if you want to be principled and responsible, you have to be able to say no. No, that is not something we want to create. No, that is not something we want to sell for that particular use to that particular user. It takes an enormous amount of self-discipline and business process to ensure that an organization operating at a global scale avoids falling into those traps. I have been encouraged when I run into an account team that worked for months to sell something and is told they cannot, and they really do get it. Still, it requires staying constantly focused on this. You can say you are principled, but if at the end of the day you will do every deal that can be done, then the only principle you are really upholding is that you will do every deal that can be done, and it ends up swallowing everything else.

points.core: Commercial momentum naturally pushes tech companies to sell products to any buyer.
points.note: Accept: default business incentives drive organizations to keep shipping products and closing sales with anyone willing to pay. Do not credit: generic claims that corporations are greedy without describing the commercial default to serve every willing buyer.

points.core: Refusing to turn down profitable deals lets revenue override every stated principle.
points.note: Accept: if a company executes every deal it legally or commercially can, deal-making becomes its only real principle and swallows all others. Do not credit: vague advice to balance profit with ethics.

points.core: Enforcing ethical boundaries at scale requires formal business processes to veto deals.
points.note: Accept: structured review gates, self-discipline, and operational governance capable of saying no to specific products, use cases, or customers even late in a sales cycle. Do not credit: relying solely on individual employee goodwill or informal norms.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Stated ethical principles collapse when they are decoupled from the structures that actually drive decisions: authority, incentives, and accountability.

Principles usually live in a document or an advisory body, while the power to ship, fund, and prioritize sits with product and business leaders who are measured on revenue, speed, and growth. When the two conflict, the measured goal wins, because nothing in the organization makes the principle binding.

Several structural features produce this. Ethics teams and review boards are typically advisory, with no veto, budget, or escalation path to the board. Principles are written abstractly ("fairness," "transparency") and never translated into concrete requirements, thresholds, or release gates, so they cannot be tested or audited. Ownership is diffuse, so no named individual answers for a violation. Performance reviews and compensation reward delivery, not restraint. And review often comes late in development, when changing course is expensive.

The result is what researchers call the principles-to-practice gap, or "ethics washing": principles function as signaling rather than constraints. They hold only where they are embedded in decision rights, metrics, and consequences.

The response ties enforceable ethical boundaries to formal review gates and decision authority capable of stopping a business decision.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
In enterprise technology governance, stated ethical principles collapse structurally when organizations treat ethics as an advisory overlay rather than an enforceable operational constraint. The primary driver is misaligned incentives: executives, product managers, and engineers are compensated and promoted on delivery speed, user growth, and revenue, turning unquantified ethical commitments into career-penalizing friction. Simultaneously, ethics functions rarely possess hard institutional power. Lacking independent budgets, structural insulation from commercial leadership, or binding veto authority at release gates, review boards are routinely bypassed or overridden when deadlines tighten.

Compounding this power asymmetry is an operational translation gap. Abstract values like fairness and transparency seldom map cleanly onto concrete engineering specifications, architectural controls, or auditable metrics, leaving developers to resolve complex trade-offs ad hoc under schedule pressure. Finally, accountability fractures across legal, security, product, and external vendor silos. Because no single decision-maker bears balance-sheet responsibility for downstream societal or systemic harm, competitive market pressure steadily erodes voluntary restraint whenever principled governance threatens short-term profitability.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The main structural cause is decoupling. A company writes its principles in one part of the organization, while decisions get made and rewarded in another. Ethics statements usually live with communications, legal, or an advisory board. Product roadmaps, budgets, launch dates and performance targets are set elsewhere and measured by growth and speed.

When a principle conflicts with a deadline or a revenue target, nothing forces the principle to win. Nobody owns it, it has no budget, it can't block a launch, it isn't measured, and breaking it costs nothing. So the incentive system decides the outcome every time.

Brent Mittelstadt's 2019 paper "Principles alone cannot guarantee ethical AI" adds that principles like "fairness" are too abstract to apply without concrete methods. Technology firms also lack a profession's fiduciary duties and enforceable codes.

You can see this when pressure arrives. Google's AI ethics council was dissolved about a week after it launched, and several large firms cut their responsible-AI teams in the 2023 layoffs.

Principles hold only when they come with real decision rights, such as launch gates or veto power, named owners who are accountable, audits, and incentives that reward following them.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
A company's stated ethical principles collapse in practice primarily because of misaligned organizational incentives and a lack of enforceable decision rights. When executive compensation, team metrics, and promotion criteria reward shipping velocity, user growth, and short-term revenue, ethical constraints become uncompensated friction that employees are implicitly pressured to bypass. Compounding this, governance bodies and ethics teams are typically structured as advisory functions rather than binding gates; without independent reporting lines, budget control, or genuine veto power over product launches, their recommendations are easily overridden during commercial crunches.

Principles also fail when abstract values like fairness or accountability are never translated into concrete engineering specifications, measurable thresholds, or mandatory controls within the software development lifecycle. Finally, organizational silos and complex technical supply chains diffuse responsibility so thoroughly that no single leader owns downstream harms, while information asymmetry shields technical trade-offs from board-level scrutiny. Without structural enforcement, clear ownership, and incentives aligned with risk reduction, ethical principles inevitably degrade into performative rhetoric.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A company’s ethical principles collapse when its governance makes them optional under pressure. If leaders are rewarded for revenue, speed, and cost savings, while the teams responsible for ethics lack the authority to delay a launch or require changes, the incentives decide which commitments survive.

The failure becomes routine when the people who benefit from an exception can approve it themselves, the costs fall on customers or workers, and nobody is accountable for the outcome. Ethical principles hold in practice when they shape who can make decisions, what those decisions are measured against, and who answers for the consequences.

The response calls for authority to delay launches or require changes and leaves unspecified a formal process with the power to reject a product, use case, or sale.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A company’s ethical principles collapse in practice when the people accountable for upholding them lack the authority to change a decision, while the people who control budgets and launches are rewarded for speed, revenue, or cost savings. A missed deadline affects a manager’s performance review. A warning about harm may carry little weight if nobody has to act on it or justify proceeding.

That imbalance makes failure predictable even when employees take the principles seriously. If an ethics team can flag a risk but product leaders can waive it without independent review, each launch can proceed as a plausible exception. Over time, those exceptions become the company’s actual policy.
